title: Snowflake at Discord
summary: Discord Snowflake IDs trade per-request consensus for deployment-time coordination: time + worker + sequence packed into 64 bits for sortable, decentralized unique IDs.
topic: Fault and Failure Tolerance + Distributed Consensus

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: A Discord Snowflake is **uniqueness without asking permission**. No database sequence, no Raft round, no lock on the hot path. Each generator stamps `time + who-am-I + counter` into 64 bits and never talks to anyone. The trade-off is explicit: you give up strict gapless ordering and absolute safety under clock misbehavior to get **independent, always-available, time-sortable ID generation at message-send rate**.
What a Discord Snowflake actually is

A Snowflake is an unsigned 64-bit integer that encodes its own creation time plus the identity of the process that made it. Discord adopted the pattern pioneered at Twitter because the naive alternatives both break at Discord scale. A central Postgres `SERIAL` or auto-increment column is a single writer, a single failure domain, and a cross-region latency tax on every message, channel, guild, role, and emoji creation. A random v4 UUID removes the bottleneck but destroys locality: IDs are unindexed chaos, you cannot sort by creation time, you cannot paginate with `after_id`, and you cannot extract age without a second column. Snowflake is the middle path chosen for a reason: pack enough timestamp in the high bits that numeric order equals time order, pack enough generator identity in the middle bits that two machines in the same millisecond never collide, and pack a per-millisecond counter in the low bits so one machine can mint thousands of IDs before the clock ticks. It is not consensus. It is the deliberate avoidance of consensus.

Concretely, Discord uses a custom epoch of `1420070400000` milliseconds, which is 1 January 2015 UTC. Every ID stores `current_time_ms - discord_epoch` in the high bits, not Unix time, which buys extra years before the timestamp field overflows. The remaining bits are split into a worker identifier, a process identifier on that worker, and a 12-bit sequence number that resets to zero each millisecond. The widely deployed split is 5 bits worker plus 5 bits process plus 12 bits sequence, giving 32 workers × 32 processes × 4096 IDs per millisecond per process. That is roughly 4 million IDs per millisecond cluster-wide in theory, over 100,000 per second per process in practice. The leading bit stays zero so the value fits in a signed 64-bit integer and survives in JavaScript, Java, Go, and JSON without precision loss. If you right-shift an ID by 22 and add the Discord epoch, you get creation time in milliseconds. That property is why clients can sort messages, infer account age, and paginate without a separate `created_at` index.

items: **High bits — timestamp:** milliseconds since Discord epoch. This is why `id1 < id2` almost always means `created1 <= created2`. Chosen because time is the only globally meaningful ordering signal you get for free.

**Middle bits — worker ID (5 bits) + process ID (5 bits):** statically assigned identity of the generator. This is where coordination lives. You coordinate once at deploy time so you never coordinate at request time.

**Low bits — sequence / increment (12 bits):** per-process counter for IDs minted in the same millisecond. Resets to 0 on millisecond rollover. This is what lets a single thread mint 4096 IDs per millisecond without a syscall.
**Zero sign bit:** keeps the value positive in signed 64-bit systems. Boring, but getting this wrong breaks JSON clients and database drivers, so it matters more than it looks.

blocks.text: Generation is a tight local loop, and that locality is the whole fault-tolerance story. A generator process holds three pieces of mutable state in memory: `last_timestamp_ms`, `sequence`, and its assigned `worker_id + process_id`. There is no RPC, no quorum check, no database round-trip. On request it samples the wall clock, compares against `last_timestamp`, and decides: if the clock moved forward, reset `sequence` to zero and stamp; if the clock is in the same millisecond, increment `sequence` and stamp; if `sequence` overflowed 4095 in that millisecond, stall until the next millisecond; if the clock moved backward, refuse to mint. Why stall and refuse instead of trying to be clever? Because any fix that reuses a prior `(timestamp, worker, sequence)` tuple creates a duplicate primary key downstream, and duplicate message IDs corrupt history permanently. Waiting 1 ms is cheap. Repairing duplicate IDs across replicas is not. That is the core trade-off made explicit in code.

blocks.title: Snowflake generation loop
blocks.caption: Local decision tree per ID — no network on the hot path.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  R[Request new ID] --> T[Read wall clock ms]
  T --> C{Compare to lastMs}
  C -->|clock moved forward| Z[sequence = 0]
  Z --> S[Stamp ID]
  C -->|same ms| I[sequence = sequence + 1]
  I --> O{sequence > 4095}
  O -->|no| S
  O -->|yes| W[Wait for next ms]
  W --> T
  C -->|clock moved backward| B[Refuse or wait]
  B --> T
  S --> E[Emit 64-bit ID]

blocks.text: Notice what is missing: leader election, log replication, fencing. Consensus systems like Raft or Paxos give you a single agreed order at the cost of availability during partitions and added latency on every write. Snowflake inverts that. It accepts that two IDs created in the same millisecond on different workers have no meaningful global order beyond timestamp tie, and in exchange every availability zone keeps minting IDs even if it is cut off from the rest of the world. Ordering within a millisecond is worker-dependent, not causal. That is acceptable for Discord messages because clients already resolve ties by sequence and because strict linearizability of creation order was never a product requirement. What the product does require — no duplicates, rough time order, survivability during network splits — is exactly what this gives. Coordination is pushed to the control plane: assigning unique 10-bit generator identities. If that assignment is correct, the data plane cannot collide unless the clock lies or the sequence overflows.

Interviewers do not want a recitation of bit widths. They want you to name what you lose when you remove coordination, and why Discord decided the loss was affordable. Every benefit below has a paired cost, and a strong candidate states both in the same breath.

blocks.caption: Snowflake design trade-offs — benefit and paired cost.
rows: No per-ID coordination
Generators never block on network; tail latency is microseconds; survives AZ and region partitions
No strict global order or gapless sequence; ties within same ms are arbitrary
Time-ordered high bits
Sort and paginate by ID alone; `WHERE id > ?` replaces timestamp index; trivial archiving
Exposes creation time publicly; leaks message rate and enables user-age scraping
Static worker + process bits
Collision-free without a central allocator on hot path; easy to trace which host minted an ID
Must guarantee uniqueness of 1024 identities; reuse after scale-up or container restart causes duplicates
12-bit per-ms sequence
4096 IDs per ms per process with no lock beyond a thread-local counter
Hard throughput ceiling per process; burst beyond 4096/ms forces artificial 1 ms stall and p99 spike
Wall-clock dependence
No logical-clock propagation; simple to implement and debug
NTP step, VM freeze, leap handling can stall or regress time; small backward jump halts minting

blocks.text: How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Snowflake failures are clock failures and identity failures, not Byzantine failures. They are mundane, which is why they pass code review and then page you at 3 AM. The most dangerous is clock regression. NTP slews, chrony steps, a VM pauses for live migration and resumes 200 ms in the past. A correct generator must not mint with a timestamp less than or equal to `last_timestamp` with a reused sequence, so it either blocks or throws. From the outside that looks like a sudden drop in send success rate on one worker while peers are healthy, with `clock_moved_backwards` counters spiking and message-create latency forming a flat plateau exactly equal to the regression window. The naive fix — clamp to `last_timestamp` and keep incrementing — only works until sequence exhausts, then you are either duplicating or stalling anyway. The opinionated stance: block and shed load rather than risk duplicate primary keys. Duplicate IDs are unrecoverable corruption; added latency is a retryable error. Second is sequence exhaustion under hot keys. One process handling a viral channel or bulk guild-create can exceed 4096 IDs in a single millisecond. Symptom is periodic 1-2 ms latency teeth on that process alone, correlated with ID rate, not CPU or GC. Fix is sharding load across processes, not widening the sequence field, because stealing bits from timestamp shortens system lifetime and stealing from worker reduces fleet size. Third is worker-ID collision after autoscaling, container reuse, or a bad config push that assigns the same 10-bit identity to two pods. Symptom is the worst kind: rare duplicate-key errors on insert, two different messages sharing an ID, pagination skipping entries. You will see it as `duplicate key value violates unique constraint` in storage, long after the bad assignment. Mitigation belongs in the control plane, not the generator: allocate worker IDs from a strongly consistent store like ZooKeeper, etcd, or a database lease at startup, refuse to start without a lease, and include worker identity in observability so collisions are attributable.

items: **Clock moved backward:** message send returns retryable error or times out on one host only; `last_timestamp > now` in logs. Cause: NTP step, VM pause. Do not mask by reusing timestamp.
**Sequence overflow:** p99 spikes in 1 ms increments on a single hot process at >4000 IDs/ms. Cause: load imbalance. Fix by spreading creators, not by widening sequence.
**Duplicate IDs in storage:** unique-constraint violations on insert, missing messages in pagination. Cause: duplicated worker/process bits. Fix by fenced allocation at boot.

**IDs jump into future:** newly minted IDs sort after messages not yet created; clients show out-of-order history. Cause: one host clock ahead. Fix by NTP monitoring and rejecting far-future timestamps.
**Exhausted timestamp bits (slow burn):** not an outage today, but choosing 41 vs 42 timestamp bits decides whether you overflow in ~69 years or ~139 years from epoch. Document the expiry.

blocks.title: Clock regression is the exam question
blocks.text: If the clock goes backward, **you must wait**. Returning an ID with a reused timestamp plus reused sequence is a duplicate. Returning an ID with an old timestamp and a fresh sequence looks safe until sequence wraps and you collide with history. The only safe moves are to stall until `now >= last_timestamp` or to fail the request. Anyone who suggests `max(now, last_timestamp)` without bounding sequence has not operated this system.

Read the code as policy, not just bit-shifting. The shift amounts `22 = 5 + 5 + 12` encode the entire capacity plan: 10 bits of fleet identity, 12 bits of burst headroom. The two branches that matter for fault tolerance are the `raise` on backward clock and the `wait` on sequence exhaustion. Both choose availability degradation over correctness violation, which is the correct priority for an ID allocator feeding an immutable message log. The `decode` helper is equally important operationally: because worker and process bits are embedded, any duplicate or future-dated ID tells you exactly which host to quarantine. That traceability is why you keep identity bits even though a pure random suffix would also avoid collisions. Randomness hides the culprit; structured identity names it. In an interview, point at those two branches and state the invariant aloud: no two calls from distinct processes ever emit the same 64-bit value unless clocks regressed or identities collided, and both of those are monitored control-plane failures, not data-plane races.
How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Start from requirements, not bits
items.text: Say: millions of IDs per second, no single point of failure, sortable by time, fits in 64 bits for Postgres BIGINT and JS number. Derive the bit split from those numbers: need ~4096/ms/process, ~1024 generators, decades of timestamps. Interviewers grade the derivation, not memorization.

items.title: Draw the hot path with no network
items.text: Sketch client -> app server -> local generator -> storage insert. Emphasize the generator is in-process. Then contrast with a ticket-server or Raft-sequenced alternative and quantify the extra round-trip per message. Name the trade-off: latency and availability versus strict ordering.

items.title: Move consensus to boot time
items.text: Explain worker-ID assignment via etcd / ZooKeeper ephemeral node or DB lease with fencing. State the rule: process refuses to serve without a unique lease. This is where you show you understand that Snowflake still needs consensus, just not per ID.

items.title: Handle the clock question head-on
items.text: Expect: what if NTP steps backward? Answer: block or fail, never reuse. Mention monotonic vs wall clock, bounding NTP slew, alerting on `now < last_ms`, and rejecting far-future timestamps on read path. This is the Medium-difficulty filter.

items.title: Close with pagination and operability
items.text: Show payoff: `GET /messages?after=<snowflake>&limit=50` with a B-tree on ID, no secondary timestamp index, trivial sharding by ID range or by guild plus ID. Add observability: emit worker/process in logs, track sequence-exhaust waits and clock regressions as first-class metrics.

items: **Snowflake IDs are globally ordered.** No. They are ordered by timestamp, but two IDs in the same millisecond from different workers have no causal order. Do not use them as a linearizability proof.
**Snowflakes need Raft per ID.** The opposite. The design exists to keep consensus off the hot path. Consensus appears once at startup for identity assignment, then gets out of the way.
**Bigger sequence field is always better.** Widening sequence steals bits from timestamp or fleet size. 12 bits already allows ~4M IDs/ms fleet-wide. If one process needs more, rebalance load first.

**UUIDv4 solves the same problem.** UUIDv4 solves uniqueness but sacrifices sortability and locality. Range scans become random I/O, pagination needs a separate cursor, and time extraction requires another column.

**Clock sync solves clock regression.** NTP reduces frequency but cannot eliminate steps, VM pauses, or operator error. The generator must still handle backward time as a correctness case, not a monitoring nicety.
**Worker ID can be hostname hash.** Hashing without coordination risks collision on restart and scale-out. Use leased allocation with expiry and fencing, and fail closed when the lease is lost.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Fit assessment for Snowflake-style IDs.
rows: You mint high-rate immutable entities (messages, events, posts) across many hosts and zones
You need gapless, auditable sequences like invoice numbers — gaps from clock stalls and restarts violate the requirement
Consumers paginate, sort, or shard by creation time and you want ID-as-cursor
Creation time must stay private — Snowflakes are decodable timestamps and leak rate and age
You can run a control plane for unique worker leases (etcd, ZooKeeper, DB)
Generators are fully ephemeral serverless functions with no stable identity and no place to lease one
64-bit storage matters (Postgres BIGINT, Snowflake partitioning, JS-safe integers)
You need unguessable IDs for capability URLs — sequential time-ordered IDs are enumerable; use random tokens instead

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Discord Snowflake packs **time plus leased generator identity plus per-millisecond sequence** into 64 bits so every host mints sortable unique IDs with no per-ID coordination — **trading strict global order and clock immunity for availability and speed, with safety resting on unique worker leases and refusing to mint when the clock regresses**.
